rows.pred_answer: The EU AI Act applies a risk-based framework with four tiers plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models. The first tier is prohibited practices: Article 5 bans eight categories of AI practice outright, including subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement except in narrowly defined circumstances, and others. The second tier is high-risk systems, reached by two cumulative routes under Article 6: a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, or where the system falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration, and administration of justice. The third tier is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency obligations, which require providers to ensure natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, to mark synthetic audio, image, video or text content in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, and require deployers to inform persons exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems and to disclose deepfake content. The fourth tier is minimal risk, for which the Regulation imposes no mandatory obligations. Running parallel to these four tiers is the general-purpose AI model regime under Articles 51 to 56: Article 51 classifies a general-purpose AI model as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, or where the Commission so designates it; Article 53 sets baseline provider duties for all general-purpose AI models; and Article 55 adds further obligations for those with systemic risk.

rows.pred_answer: The EU AI Act applies a risk-based framework with four tiers plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models. The first tier is prohibited practices: Article 5 bans eight categories of AI practice outright, including subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement except in narrowly defined circumstances, and others. The second tier is high-risk systems, reached by two cumulative routes under Article 6: a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, or where the system falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration, and administration of justice. The third tier is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency obligations, which require providers to ensure natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, to mark synthetic audio, image, video or text content in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, and require deployers to inform persons exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems and to disclose deepfake content. The fourth tier is minimal risk, for which the Regulation imposes no mandatory obligations. Running parallel to these four tiers is the general-purpose AI model regime under Articles 51 to 56: Article 51 classifies a general-purpose AI model as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, or where the Commission so designates it; Article 53 sets baseline provider duties for all general-purpose AI models; and Article 55 adds further obligations for those with systemic risk.
